content: Contraceptive education is a standard part of postpartum care, but its effectiveness is rarely evaluated. These programs are based on the assumption that postpartum women are motivated to use contraception and may not return to healthcare providers for family planning advice. Women often wish to discuss contraception both during pregnancy and after being discharged from the hospital. However, two-thirds of postpartum women have unmet contraceptive needs. In the United States, many adolescent mothers experience repeat pregnancies within a year of giving birth. The objective of this review was to assess the effectiveness of educational interventions for postpartum women regarding contraceptive use. To achieve this, randomized controlled trials (RCTs) were considered, provided the intervention began within one month after delivery. The search for relevant studies was conducted across multiple databases, including PubMed, CENTRAL, CINAHL, POPLINE, and Web of Science, up to June 2015. Additional searches were performed in ClinicalTrials.gov and ICTRP for ongoing trials. Earlier searches also included EMBASE and PsycInfo, and reference lists of relevant articles were reviewed. Investigators were contacted to locate additional reports for earlier versions of the review. The review included RCTs that examined postpartum contraceptive education delivered to individuals or groups. Cluster-randomized trials were eligible if the analysis accounted for clustering. Data from the studies were abstracted and analyzed using Review Manager. For dichotomous outcomes, the Mantel-Haenszel odds ratio (OR) with a 95% confidence interval (CI) was calculated. For continuous variables, the mean difference (MD) with a 95% CI was computed. Due to the variability in interventions and outcome measures, a meta-analysis was not conducted. Twelve trials met the eligibility criteria, including three added in the most recent update. These studies involved a total of 4,145 women. Eight trials were conducted in the United States, while the others were from Australia, Nepal, Pakistan, and Syria. Four studies provided a single educational session before hospital discharge, three involved structured counseling of varying intensity, and one used informal counseling. Among eight interventions with more than one contact, five focused on adolescents. Of these, three involved home visits, one provided multiple clinic services, and one included in-person contact and phone follow-up. For women of varying ages, two interventions involved home visits, and one included phone follow-up. A sensitivity analysis was conducted on six trials with moderate or high-quality evidence. In one study involving adolescents, those who received home-based mentoring had fewer second births within two years compared to the control group (OR 0.41, 95% CI 0.17 to 1.00). However, the other five interventions showed no significant effect. Among trials with lower-quality evidence, two demonstrated some effectiveness. In Nepal, women who received an educational session immediately postpartum were more likely to use contraception at six months compared to those who received a later or no session (OR 1.62, 95% CI 1.06 to 2.50). In an Australian study, adolescents in a structured home-visiting program were more likely to use effective contraception at six months compared to those receiving standard home visits (OR 3.24, 95% CI 1.35 to 7.79). The authors concluded that the overall quality of evidence in this review was moderate to low, and the effectiveness of the interventions was generally low. Improvements in program design and implementation are needed. Many studies did not report details such as provider training, adherence to intervention protocols, or measurement of participants' knowledge and skills. Additionally, many trials lacked objective outcome measures, such as pregnancy tests or structured questionnaires for contraceptive use. Valid and reliable outcome measures are essential for obtaining meaningful results. However, given the associated costs and logistical challenges, some programs may not be feasible in all settings.
